meta.reportLabel: Sun - THE NON-CONFIRMATION RESOLVED, AND IT RESOLVED AGAINST THE DOLLAR. Friday's US retail sales fell 0.6% m/m against +0.1% expected - the steepest drop since May 2025 - and Michigan preliminary sentiment collapsed to 51.0 from 55.2, and this time everything traded it. The dollar index closed -0.27% at a one-week low, EUR/USD broke its 100-DMA at 1.1566 to a two-month high in the upper 1.15s, GBP/USD hit a three-month high at 1.3560, gold rallied to 4,373 and pushed at 4,400, silver held 64.53. September hike odds are 32%. That is four consecutive US prints - payrolls -23k, CPI 3.4%, PPI 4.7%, retail sales -0.6% - all pointing the same way, and the price has finally stopped refusing them: USD is downgraded to -2 WEAKENING, DXY flips from RANGE to SHORT, and XAU/USD goes back to LONG. The awkward exception is the yen, which had its BIGGEST WEEKLY LOSS IN THREE MONTHS at 159.43 and has erased half the gains from the historic joint intervention - so USD/JPY is a low-conviction short only because 160 is where the MoF lives, not because the tape agrees. Oil fell to WTI 80.96 into an IEA report saying global stocks dropped 2.2mb/d in July and the deficit is now 1.8mb/d, with Hormuz throughput still at an eighth of pre-war. Cleanest trades: EUR/USD LONG, EUR/NZD LONG, AUD/NZD LONG, GBP/NZD LONG, USD/CHF SHORT. Japan Q2 GDP tonight at 23:50Z is the week's first test.

meta.regime: The regime is policy differentials, and this weekend it stopped being a regime with an asterisk. For two weeks this book has been carrying the same uncomfortable observation: the US data was deteriorating print after print and the dollar would not go down. Friday ended that. July retail sales contracted 0.6% m/m against a consensus +0.1% and a prior +0.2%, the largest single-month drop in more than a year, and the University of Michigan preliminary sentiment index for August fell about 8% to 51.0 from 55.2, with households explicitly citing Middle East-driven prices. The dollar index closed down 0.27% at a one-week low, EUR/USD cleared its 100-day moving average at 1.1566 and printed a two-month high in the upper 1.15s, GBP/USD reached 1.3560 for a three-month high, gold recovered to about 4,373 and pressed the 4,400 handle, and silver held 64.53. Money markets now price roughly a 32% chance of a September hike, down from 35% Thursday and 55% a week ago. The dollar is downgraded from -1 to -2 WEAKENING and the dollar-short book gets its conviction back: DXY flips from RANGE to SHORT, XAU/USD from RANGE to LONG, USD/CHF from LOW-MED to a MEDIUM short. The one leg that did not cooperate is the yen. USD/JPY sat at 159.43 into the weekend and the yen posted its biggest weekly loss in three months, erasing roughly half the gains from the record joint MoF/US Treasury intervention, even as Reuters reporting has all but locked a BoJ hike to 1.25% on September 17-18. A currency that weakens into a near-certain hike is a currency being pushed by carry, not by policy, and the MoF sits at 160. Oil is the other disconnect: WTI slipped to 80.96 and Brent held near 87 on hopes for an Iran-Oman shipping-lane framework, while the IEA reported global stocks fell 2.2 million b/d in July to under 7.9 billion barrels and doubled its deficit estimate to 1.8 million b/d, and Hormuz throughput remains about an eighth of pre-war.

dailyRead: The two-week standoff between the US data and the US dollar broke on Friday, and it broke the way the data had been pointing. July retail sales fell 0.6% month-on-month against a consensus of +0.1% and a June reading of +0.2% - the steepest contraction in more than a year - and the University of Michigan preliminary sentiment index for August dropped roughly 8% to 51.0 from 55.2, ending a two-month recovery, with respondents naming Middle East-driven prices as the reason. What matters is not the prints themselves but that everything finally traded them. The dollar index closed 0.27% lower at a one-week low. EUR/USD cleared its 100-day moving average at 1.1566 and printed a fresh two-month high in the upper 1.15s. GBP/USD reached 1.3560, a three-month high. Gold recovered to roughly 4,373 and pushed at the 4,400 threshold on falling front-end yields, and silver held 64.53 after Thursday's slide. September hike odds fell to about 32% from 35% Thursday and 55% a week earlier. Set that against the sequence: July payrolls CONTRACTED 23,000 with the prior two months revised down 146,000 and average hourly earnings at 3.2% y/y; July CPI 3.4% headline and 2.5% core; July PPI 4.7% against 5.0% expected with core at 4.2% and the monthly index flat; and now the consumer rolling over in both spending and sentiment. That is four consecutive prints in the same direction with price confirmation on the last one, and it is enough to move USD from -1 to -2 WEAKENING. Practically: DXY flips from RANGE to a MEDIUM SHORT, XAU/USD comes off RANGE back to LONG, XAG/USD upgrades to a low-conviction LONG with the caveat that its industrial leg is being dragged by soft Chinese demand, and USD/CHF becomes a MEDIUM short rather than a LOW-MED one. EUR/USD is the cleanest expression and stays HIGH. The exception that has to be respected is the yen. USD/JPY finished the week at 159.43 and the yen posted its BIGGEST WEEKLY LOSS IN THREE MONTHS, giving back roughly half the gains from the record joint MoF/US Treasury operation at the end of July. That happened in the same week Reuters reported that the intervention plus Treasury Secretary Bessent's stated preference for an early Japanese move have all but locked a BoJ hike to 1.25% at the September 17-18 meeting. A currency that sells off into a near-certain hike is being driven by carry and positioning, not policy, and 160 is where the Ministry of Finance has already shown it will act. So JPY holds at -1 MIXED, USD/JPY is a SHORT only at LOW-MED conviction and only because of the intervention line rather than the tape, JPYBASKET stays RANGE per the MIXED verdict, and the yen crosses stay LONG at MEDIUM at best. Japan's Q2 GDP lands tonight at 23:50Z and is the first real test of that framework. The euro keeps the top score at +2 and its case is unchanged and self-supporting: July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5% and services at 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, deposit facility 2.25% re-verified on TE this morning against the 2.40% refi headline, composite PMI 52.0, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3%, ZEW 23.4. September 10 is still around 70% priced. The caution I flagged on Friday stands and has not worsened: TE's ECB commentary describes the post-July tone as wait-and-see, euro-area consumer inflation expectations fell to 3.0% from 3.5%, producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y with the monthly index at -0.3%, and June retail sales were -0.3% m/m. The hike is the base case; the meeting is not a formality. Australia holds +2 on the August Statement on Monetary Policy - underlying inflation 3.3% by end-2026, no return to the 2-3% midpoint until early 2028, risks skewed UP - with the cash rate at 4.35%, the highest in the G10, Q2 weighted median CPI at 3.7% from 3.5%, services inflation 4.0%, employment +76,343 and unemployment 4.4%. The dovish crack is still July consumer inflation expectations at 4.7% from 5.5% and Assistant Governor Kent's 'somewhat restrictive' framing. Sterling stays +1 and had a good week - Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q with the y/y rate ACCELERATING to 1.2% from 0.9%, unemployment 4.9%, wages 4.3% including bonuses, employment +148,000, a 6-3 hold on July 30 with three dissenters - but the June trade deficit widened to GBP 5.54bn from 1.04bn and RICS house prices sit at -30, and the Aug 18 labour report at 06:00Z followed by July CPI on Aug 19 will decide whether 1.3560 was a top or a base. Canada stays +1 with the best labour print in the G10 (+75,100 in July, unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4%, participation 65.1%) and CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9% both BELOW target, but the terms-of-trade leg keeps thinning as crude fades - terms of trade 101 from 107, oil exports CAD 13.26bn from 14.92bn - and Tuesday's July CPI at 12:30Z is the input. Switzerland stays at 0 MIXED after the Q2 GDP shock of +1.5% q/q against 0.2-0.4% expected; the pharma-driven distortion caveat stands, but with CPI at 0.4%, PPI at -2.1% and the policy rate at zero, the franc is a funding currency with a growth story rather than a free short, which is why the CHF crosses sit at MEDIUM and LOW-MED. New Zealand remains the cleanest fundamental short at -2 - Q3 two-year business inflation expectations at 2.34% against a 2.7% forecast and 2.53% prior, unemployment 5.6% and the highest since 2015, wage growth 2.1%, ANZ commodity prices decelerating to +0.5% y/y, Global Dairy Trade up only 0.1% - but be honest about Friday: the kiwi RALLIED on dollar weakness. That is why NZD/USD moves from SHORT to RANGE (two weak currencies do not make a trade) while EUR/NZD, AUD/NZD and GBP/NZD stay the HIGH-conviction expressions of the same view. Finally the oil complex, where the disconnect widened rather than closed. WTI slipped to 80.96 and Brent held near 87 as Iran and Oman moved into the final stages of a shipping-lane framework - but Tehran has been explicit that a lanes agreement is not a return to normal transit, national security chief Zolghadr's list of demands still includes lifting the naval blockade, withdrawing forces, ending the war permanently, compensation and unfreezing assets, and the blockade remains in place. Meanwhile the IEA reported global stocks fell 2.2 million b/d in July to below 7.9 billion barrels for the first time since early 2025, and doubled its projected deficit to 1.8 million b/d, while physical Hormuz throughput runs at roughly an eighth of pre-war volume. The market is pricing a reopening that has not happened against a physical balance that is tightening. USOIL stays RANGE, but the risk in that range is asymmetric to the upside and a failed framework is the single largest unpriced event on the board. Copper is the counterweight - 6.59 USD/lb, near record highs at about USD 14,070/t but sliding on soft Chinese demand, with China industrial production and retail sales at 02:00Z Monday the immediate test for the XCU long and for the Aussie behind it.

today.headline: Retail sales -0.6% and Michigan 51.0 finally broke the dollar: DXY -0.27% to a one-week low.
today.read: Four consecutive prints now point the same way and the price has stopped arguing - hold and add to dollar shorts through EUR and CHF rather than through the yen. Jackson Hole on Aug 27 is the only scheduled event that can reverse this before the Sept 16 FOMC.

today.read: The technical break confirms a fundamental view that has not changed in three weeks, so this is a hold-and-run rather than a new entry. The Sept 10 ECB at ~70% priced is what the position is really levered to.

USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. Every input since has cut the same way, and Friday added price confirmation for the first time. Aug 7 payrolls: July nonfarm payrolls CONTRACTED by 23,000 against +83,000 to +95,000 expected, with the prior two months revised down by a combined 146,000; the fall in unemployment to 4.1% from 4.2% is a participation artefact at a five-year-low 61.4% participation, and average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2% y/y. Aug 12 CPI: 3.4% headline from 3.5%, core 2.5% from 2.6%, both at consensus, +0.1% m/m with shelter about two thirds of it and no visible pass-through from crude. Aug 13 PPI: final demand 4.7% y/y against 5.0% expected and 5.5% in June, core 4.2% from 4.7%, the monthly index FLAT. Aug 14, the decisive one: July retail sales -0.6% m/m against +0.1% expected and +0.2% prior, the largest drop in over a year, and the University of Michigan preliminary August sentiment index at 51.0 from 55.2, an 8% fall that ended a two-month recovery, with respondents citing Middle East-linked prices. TE carries the policy rate at 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4%, core 2.5%, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised, GDP annual 2.1%, unemployment 4.1%, initial claims 209,000. Money markets price roughly 32% for September, down from 35% Thursday and 55% a week ago. The committee is openly split - Barkin argues hold on cooling inflation, Hammack still wants to raise now, Cook says she is prepared to - but the balance of evidence has moved decisively toward the doves and the dollar index finally closed down 0.27% at a one-week low on it. Jackson Hole on Aug 27 is where Warsh has to say whether the deferred energy tail still counts, and it is now the single biggest event for the dollar.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (~70% priced, still not a formality)
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, main refinancing 2.40% and marginal lending 2.65%, confirmed unchanged on Jul 23 and re-verified on TE this morning - use the 2.25% depo, not the 2.40% headline. TE's model still carries 2.65% on the refi by end-September, i.e. one more 25bp move. The domestic case is why EUR holds the top score and it stands on its own: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% and services inflation 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, final composite PMI 52.0 with services 51.7 and manufacturing 51.9, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3% and stable, ZEW 23.4 from 9.5, energy inflation accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, capacity utilisation 78.5. Lagarde's July framing - that the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they drive broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects - survives Brent near 87. EUR/USD cleared its 100-day moving average at 1.1566 on Friday to a two-month high in the upper 1.15s, which is a technical confirmation of a fundamental view rather than a new one. The standing caution: TE's ECB coverage characterises the post-July stance as explicit wait-and-see, citing softer inflation, wage growth, activity AND inflation expectations, and euro-area consumer inflation expectations fell to 3.0% from 3.5%. Pipeline disinflation is real - producer prices decelerating to 4.6% y/y from 5.9% with the monthly index at -0.3%, food inflation 1.2%, June retail sales -0.3% m/m, industrial production flat. September 10 is a real meeting and the euro's +2 is levered to it.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus, verified on TE today. The data vacuum has filled firm on the parts that matter to the MPC. Labour report: unemployment 4.9% with 1.76 million unemployed, wages 4.3% including bonuses and 3.4% excluding, real pay positive at 1.3% and 0.4%, employment change +148,000 from +99,000. Q2 GDP: +0.4% q/q against +0.3% expected, a slowdown from Q1's +0.6% but with the y/y rate ACCELERATING to 1.2% from 0.9%, and June monthly GDP +0.3% against an expected decline. June CPI 2.6% headline and 2.6% core with services at 3.6%, producer prices 3.5%. An economy accelerating on a y/y basis does not fold three dissenters on the most inflation-sensitive committee in the G10, and TE's end-of-quarter forecast is 4.00%. GBP/USD reached 1.3560 on Friday, a three-month high, on the dollar leg rather than the sterling one. The offsets are real and unresolved: the June trade deficit widened sharply to GBP 5.54bn from 1.04bn against a 3.6bn forecast, industrial production was soft, the RICS house price balance sits at -30, vacancies are at 712,000 below pre-pandemic levels, economic inactivity is rising to 9.11 million at a 20.9% rate and the claimant count rose 6.7k from 1.3k. The Aug 18 labour report at 06:00Z and July CPI on Aug 19 decide whether the +1 survives and whether 1.3560 was a top.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (near-locked - and the yen fell into it anyway)
JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. The policy path moved forward a month on Aug 12-13: July PPI held at 7.2% y/y with the yen-based import price index up 29.1% y/y after 30.1% in June - the currency's own weakness feeding straight into domestic prices - and Reuters reported that the record joint Japan-US intervention combined with Treasury Secretary Bessent's stated desire for an early Japanese hike have all but locked a move to 1.25% at the September 17-18 meeting, one day after the FOMC. The domestic case is the best in three decades: June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y with base pay accelerating to 3.4%, real earnings including bonuses +1.6% and positive for a sixth month, nominal growth above 3% for five straight months (longest run in 34 years); June CPI 1.7% from 1.5% with core 1.6% and core-core 1.7%; Tokyo July CPI 2.0% from 1.7%, Tokyo core 1.9% from 1.6%, Tokyo ex food and energy 2.0%; inflation expectations 2.7% from 2.4%. And the yen still had its BIGGEST WEEKLY LOSS IN THREE MONTHS, finishing at 159.43 and giving back roughly half the gains from the historic joint operation. That is the whole trade in one sentence: a currency selling off into a near-certain hike is being driven by carry and positioning, not policy. Structurally the weakness has support - trade balance -JPY 407bn, current account -JPY 923bn from +3,968bn, terms of trade deteriorating to 81.62 from 82.71, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18. But 160 is where the MoF has already shown it will act, and the policy tail into Sept 18 is now real. JPY stays -1 MIXED: short the yen small, through the crosses, and not into 160. Q2 GDP lands tonight at 23:50Z; July national CPI around Aug 20 at 23:30Z.

AUD.note: Held the cash rate at 4.35% on Aug 11 as all 37 Reuters economists expected, verified on TE today, and the tone did the work: Bullock said the domestic economy is operating ABOVE CAPACITY and that growth will need to slow to bring inflation down, and the statement retained 'including increasing the cash rate target further if required' with no qualification. The August Statement on Monetary Policy is the hawkish anchor and nothing has touched it - underlying inflation forecast at 3.3% by end-2026, no return to the middle of the 2-3% band until early 2028, and risks to inflation explicitly skewed to the UPSIDE, citing elevated energy prices and strong AI-related demand. That is the highest policy rate in the G10 after three hikes in 2026, and TE's model carries 4.60%. Q2 detail supports the hawks: headline CPI cooled to 3.8% from 4.0% and trimmed mean rose to 3.6% from 3.5%, but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%. Labour is solid - employment +76,343, unemployment 4.4%, participation 67.0%, employment rate 64.0%. July PMIs: services 53.6, composite 53.2, manufacturing 52.0; consumer confidence 83.9 and +4.1% m/m; commodity prices +15.4% y/y from 14.6%. Against it, Assistant Governor Kent said policy is only 'somewhat restrictive' and named the Australian dollar's own appreciation as part of the restraint, and the market read him as more dovish than the substance justified. The dovish crack remains July consumer inflation expectations at 4.7% from 5.5%, and the near-term risk is Chinese demand - copper slid on soft China data expectations and China industrial production and retail sales print at 02:00Z Monday.

NZD.when: Sept 2 (the hike is off; the survey settled it)
NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, verified on TE, and that cycle is finished. The RBNZ quarterly survey was the confirmation and it missed badly: Q3 two-year business inflation expectations came in at 2.34% against a 2.7% FORECAST and 2.53% prior, the lowest since Q4 2025, with one-year expectations collapsing to 2.60% from 3.41% - one of the largest single-quarter falls in the series. Only the five- and ten-year tails ticked up, to 2.31% and 2.20%. The risk this book had flagged against the kiwi short was a JUMP in expectations forcing a rethink; it went decisively the other way, which says the imported-inflation channel that drove Q2 CPI to 4.1% - 27.5% of it petrol - is not reaching what businesses actually expect, and WTI has since fallen to 80.96. The labour side is the worst in the G10: Q2 unemployment 5.6% against 5.4% expected, the highest since Q3 2015, unemployed persons 171,000, wage growth just 2.1% y/y, employment +0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%, youth unemployment 17.2%. Core inflation 3.2%. The domestic-sentiment offset is genuine - July ANZ business confidence 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence 99.3, manufacturing PMI 59.7, composite 53.6 - but ANZ commodity prices decelerated to +0.5% y/y from +2.7% and the Global Dairy Trade index rose only 0.1%, so the terms-of-trade support is gone. The honest caveat for the coming week: the kiwi RALLIED on Friday on pure dollar weakness, which is why NZD/USD moves to RANGE and the short is expressed against EUR, AUD and GBP instead.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting, re-verified on TE this morning, and the inflation side keeps it there - June CPI 2.8% from 3.2% with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%, both BELOW target, core at 2.1% and CPI-common 2.6%, and the monthly index at -0.4%. The labour leg is intact and still the best in the G10: July employment rose 75,100, the largest gain in two years, with full-time +38,600 and part-time +36,600, unemployment falling to a two-year low of 6.4% from 6.5%, participation rising to 65.1%, employment rate 60.9% and youth unemployment down to 12.6%. Wage growth is a soft 3.4% y/y with average hourly earnings at CAD 38.61, which is why this is a growth story and not a rate one. The commodity leg keeps thinning: WTI slipped to 80.96 with Brent near 87, terms of trade have fallen to 101 from 107, commodity prices decelerated to +20.7% y/y from 33.4%, and oil exports dropped to CAD 13.26bn from 14.92bn - all while tankers are still being attacked in the strait, which tells you the market has priced a reopening. Offsetting that, the trade surplus widened to CAD 3.86bn, manufacturing PMI is 53.5, small-business sentiment jumped to 58.3 and USD/CAD is pressing 1.3800 from above on the dollar leg. Q1 GDP flat at 0.0% q/q with GDP annual -0.1% and monthly GDP +0.2% in June. July CPI and BoC core CPI both land Tuesday Aug 17 at 12:30Z and are the next real input.

CHF.note: Policy rate 0.00%, verified on TE, and the SNB's own guidance has been that it is at the effective floor with FX intervention rather than rates as the active instrument. The picture is a genuine mix. On the weak side: July CPI 0.4% from 0.5% with core at 0.3% and the monthly index at -0.1%, harmonised inflation 0.7%, producer and import prices deflating at -2.1% y/y, food inflation -1.3%, unemployment drifting up to 3.0% from 2.9% with 139,276 unemployed and job vacancies falling to 45,156, and Q1 industrial production at -7.1%. On the strong side, and this is what changed on Friday the 14th: SECO's preliminary Q2 estimate put GDP growth at +1.5% q/q in real terms against a consensus range of 0.2-0.4%, the strongest print in years, driven by chemicals and pharmaceuticals. The caveat is not buried - Swiss pharma exports have been distorted for two quarters by exporters front-running US tariffs, so some of this reverses - but it lands on top of a services PMI at 63.9 from 59.8, manufacturing PMI 53.2, business confidence 104, ZEW at +10 from -25 and inflation expectations up to 1.24% from 0.69%. A zero-rate currency with a current account at 7.1% of GDP and a growth story is a funding currency you do not short with size. CHF stays at 0 MIXED, the crosses stay at MEDIUM and LOW-MED, and USD/CHF is a MEDIUM short purely on the dollar leg.

geopolitics: The oil complex is now trading a reopening that has not happened against a physical balance that is getting tighter, and that gap is the largest unpriced risk on the board. WTI slipped to 80.96 into the weekend and Brent held near 87, giving back ground after six straight higher sessions, on reports that Iran and Oman have reached the final stages of a framework covering shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has been explicit that a shipping-lane agreement is not the same thing as a return to normal transit: national security chief Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr's standing list of preconditions for reopening includes lifting the US naval blockade, withdrawing military forces, permanently ending the war, compensation for damages and the release of frozen assets, and Iran's foreign ministry has repeated that as long as the blockade continues the conditions for reopening do not exist. The blockade, reimposed after the collapse of the mid-June US-Iran memorandum, is still in place. Against that, the physical data got worse, not better: the IEA reported on Aug 12 that global oil inventories fell 2.2 million barrels a day in July, pushing total stocks below 7.9 billion barrels for the first time since early 2025, and doubled its projected deficit to 1.8 million barrels a day; physical tanker throughput through the strait is running at roughly an eighth of pre-war volume, and the limited traffic that does move is confined to specific approved corridors under local oversight rather than through the deep-water channel. Two ADNOC vessels were attacked in the strait on Aug 13 and the UAE publicly blamed Iran. The FX read has three parts. First, the falling crude price is quietly removing the strongest argument for the hawks everywhere - it is why New Zealand's business inflation expectations collapsed to 2.34%, why US PPI printed 4.7% with final demand goods down 0.7% on energy, and why the ECB's own second-round-effects framing is losing force at Brent 87 rather than 92. Second, it keeps thinning the Canadian dollar's terms-of-trade support: terms of trade at 101 from 107, oil exports at CAD 13.26bn from 14.92bn, commodity prices decelerating to +20.7% y/y from 33.4%. Third, and most important for risk management, the asymmetry runs the other way - if the corridor concessions lapse or the framework fails, the repricing is violent and it hits the CHF and JPY haven bids, the CAD long and every risk-on carry cross in the book simultaneously. Note that the Michigan sentiment collapse to 51.0 explicitly cited Middle East-driven prices, which is the first clear evidence that the energy shock is reaching US household expectations even as it fails to reach the producer price index.
